nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the critic of the great tradition and the founder of the Cambridge school
literary_identity: Critic; the editor of Scrutiny and the author of The Great Tradition and Revaluation.
biography: Born Frank Raymond Leavis at Cambridge on 14 July 1895; he served in the war, took his degree at Cambridge and taught there, founding the journal Scrutiny in 1932. Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture (1930), New Bearings in English Poetry (1932) and Revaluation (1936) made him the most feared critic in England, and The Great Tradition (1948) fixed the canon of the English novel. He held the readership at Cambridge until 1962 and died there on 14 April 1978.
literary_profile: F. R. Leavis is the most influential English critic of the twentieth century: the polemic of Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture made the defence of the minority culture the task of criticism, New Bearings in English Poetry revalued the modern poets, Revaluation and The Great Tradition fixed the canons of the verse and the novel, and the school of Scrutiny trained the teachers of English for a generation.
stylistic_characteristics: The polemical sentence of the moral urgency; the quotation examined word by word in the argument; the verdict delivered as a definition; the rejection of the historical and the sociological in favour of the valuation; the canon as the instrument of the discipline.
intellectual_concerns: The minority culture against the mass civilisation; the valuation and the canon; the great tradition of the English novel from Austen to James; the revaluation of the English poets; the discipline of English as a defence of the civilisation; the war and the loss of the organic community.
historical_significance: F. R. Leavis is the most influential English critic of the twentieth century: Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture made the defence of the minority culture the task of criticism, Revaluation and The Great Tradition fixed the canons of the verse and the novel, and the school of Scrutiny trained the teachers of English for a generation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the critic of the reading public and the historian of the popular novel
literary_identity: Critic; the author of Fiction and the Reading Public and the critic of Scrutiny.
biography: Born Quesie Dorothy Roth at London on 14 September 1906; she read English at Cambridge, married F. R. Leavis in 1929, and published Fiction and the Reading Public in 1932, the study of the bestseller and the reading habit that founded the sociology of English reading. Her essays in Scrutiny and her editions of the Victorian novelists, with her study of the country house novel, made her the historian of the popular fiction of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; she died at Cambridge on 17 August 1981.
literary_profile: Q. D. Leavis founded the sociology of English reading: Fiction and the Reading Public traced the division of the reading public into the highbrow, the middlebrow and the lowbrow and made the bestseller and the circulating library the objects of criticism, and her essays on the Victorian and the country house novel recovered the popular fiction of the nineteenth century for the discipline.
stylistic_characteristics: The sociological survey carried in the critical sentence; the bestseller and the library catalogue as the evidence; the division of the reading public stated as a diagnosis; the quotation from the popular novel read against the canon; the polemic of the standard.
intellectual_concerns: The reading public and its divisions; the bestseller, the circulating library and the bookshop; the popular novel of the nineteenth century; the country house and the woman's novel; the standard of the canon against the habit of the market.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the scholar of the Elizabethan world picture and of Milton
literary_identity: Scholar; the author of The Elizabethan World Picture and The Miltonic Setting.
biography: Born Edgar Merion Wilson Tillyard at Cambridge on 24 March 1889; he took his degrees at Cambridge and held the chair of English at Durham and then the readership at Cambridge. The Miltonic Setting (1938) and The Elizabethan World Picture (1943) made the doctrine of the order and of the correspondence the common property of the readers of the period, and his Shakespeare's Last Plays (1938) and The Elizabethan World Picture fixed the terms of the study of the Renaissance imagination; he died at Newcastle on 12 December 1962.
literary_profile: E. M. W. Tillyard is the scholar who gave the twentieth century its account of the Elizabethan world picture: his books on the great chain of being, the correspondences and the order made the doctrine the common key to the reading of Shakespeare, Donne and Milton, and the famous debate with C. S. Lewis on the personal heresy fixed the method of the period study.
stylistic_characteristics: The exposition of the doctrine in the plain ordered sentence; the diagram of the chain and the correspondence carried in the prose; the quotation from the schoolbooks and the sermons as the evidence of the common belief; the lecture manner of the scholar addressing the general reader.
intellectual_concerns: The great chain of being and the doctrine of order; the correspondences of the macrocosm and the microcosm; Milton and the Puritan imagination; the Elizabethan schoolbook and the common belief; the debate on the personal heresy in the reading of poetry.
historical_significance: E. M. W. Tillyard gave the twentieth century its account of the Elizabethan world picture: his books on the chain of being and the correspondences made the doctrine the common key to the reading of Shakespeare, Donne and Milton, and his Miltonic Setting remains the standard introduction to the Puritan imagination.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Georgian poet, the parodist and the editor of the London Mercury
literary_identity: Poet, parodist and editor; the editor of the London Mercury and the parodist of Collected Parodies.
biography: Born John Collings Squire at Plymouth on 14 November 1884; he was literary editor of the New Statesman from 1913 and editor of the London Mercury from 1919 to 1934, the house journal of the Georgian poets. His verse - The Three Hills (1913), The Survival of the Fittest (1916), Poems in One Volume (1926) - and his parodies in Collected Parodies (1921) made him the most popular versifier of the between-wars years; he was knighted in 1949 and died at Chobham, Surrey, on 30 March 1958.
literary_profile: J. C. Squire is the editor of the London Mercury and the parodist of the Georgian age: his magazine gave the Georgian poets their house journal for fifteen years, his Collected Parodies remain among the most accomplished parodies in English, and his own verse, with the early protest of The Survival of the Fittest, is the record of the Georgian lyric at its most popular.
stylistic_characteristics: The polished Georgian lyric of the landscape and the season; the parody that reproduces the manner exactly and turns it one degree; the editorial prose of the house journal; the long poem of the moon and the hills; the verse of the popular magazine.
intellectual_concerns: The Georgian lyric and its magazine; the parody as criticism; the literary journalism of the between-wars years; the war protest of 1916; the quarrel with the modernists as the editor of the traditional verse.
historical_significance: J. C. Squire is the editor of the London Mercury and the parodist of the Georgian age: his magazine gave the Georgian poets their house journal for fifteen years and his Collected Parodies remain among the most accomplished parodies in English.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Shropshire novelist of Precious Bane and the nature romance
literary_identity: Novelist; the Shropshire writer of Precious Bane and Gone to Earth.
biography: Born Mary Gladys Meredith at Leighton, Shropshire, on 25 March 1881; she lived in the Shropshire hills and wrote the novels of the county - The Golden Arrow (1916), Gone to Earth (1917), The House in Dorset (1920), Seven for a Secret (1922) - until Precious Bane (1924), with its harelipped narrator and its bargain for the land, won the Femina prize and, after Stanley Baldwin's praise in 1928, a national public. She died at St Leonards-on-Sea on 8 October 1927.
literary_profile: Mary Webb is the Shropshire novelist of the English nature romance: Precious Bane, with its harelipped narrator Prue Sarn and its bargain for the land, is the most read provincial novel of the 1920s, and Gone to Earth carried the nature romance into the tragedy of the hunted creature. Her prose of the hills, the weather and the soul made the county a world.
stylistic_characteristics: The charged prose of the nature romance, the landscape as the soul's weather; the first-person narrator of the county speech; the bargain, the curse and the chapel set against the hill and the mere; the image drawn from the farm, the loom and the storm; the elegy of the hunted creature.
intellectual_concerns: The Shropshire hills and the mere; the bargain for the land and the price of the soul; the nonconformist chapel and the old religion of the hills; the woman and the hunted creature; nature as the moral weather of the novel.
historical_significance: Mary Webb is the Shropshire novelist of the English nature romance: Precious Bane, with its harelipped narrator and its bargain for the land, is the most read provincial novel of the 1920s, and her prose of the hills and the soul made the county a world.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Westmorland novelist of the fell farm and the dalesfolk
literary_identity: Novelist; the Westmorland writer of The Lonely Plough and Old Vicarage, Grantley.
biography: Born Constance Holme in Lancashire on 2 December 1880, of a Westmorland farming family; she lived at Kendal and wrote the novels of the fell farm and the dalesfolk - The Lonely Plough (1920), Old Vicarage, Grantley (1921), The Trysting Place (1922), Green Harvest (1926) - in the prose of the fell weather and the farming year. Her books were reissued in the 1940s and she died at Kendal on 20 January 1955.
literary_profile: Constance Holme is the Westmorland novelist of the fell farm: The Lonely Plough and Old Vicarage, Grantley recorded the dalesfolk, the farming year and the fell weather in a prose of the place that made her the most exact of the regional novelists of the 1920s, and her recovery in the 1940s made her the test case of the neglected regional woman novelist.
stylistic_characteristics: The prose of the fell weather, the farming year and the stone; the dialogue of the dalesfolk in the local speech; the household and the farm as the whole of the world; the slow season as the plot; the elegy of the last of the line.
intellectual_concerns: The Westmorland fell and the dalesfolk; the farming year and the stone of the wall; the last of the line and the inheritance of the farm; the woman of the farmhouse; the region as the world entire.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Northamptonshire novelist of the country and the war
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of The Poacher and Fair Stood the Wind for France.
biography: Born Herbert Ernest Bates at Rushden, Northamptonshire, on 4 June 1905; he left school at eighteen for journalism and published his first novel in 1926. The Poacher (1935) and A House of Women (1936) made him the novelist of the Northamptonshire country, and Fair Stood the Wind for France (1944) the most read novel of the airman in the war; his short stories and his creation of the Larkin family followed after the war. He died at Canterbury on 29 January 1974.
literary_profile: H. E. Bates is the novelist of the English country and of the airman's war: The Poacher carried the country novel of the county into the 1930s in a prose of the field and the season, A House of Women made the household of women a novel of the decade, and Fair Stood the Wind for France is the most read novel of the airman behind the lines.
stylistic_characteristics: The prose of the field, the season and the weather, charged but never purple; the country county and its poacher, its farm and its market; the household of women and the man who enters it; the airman's France in the novel of escape; the short story of the single observed moment.
intellectual_concerns: The English country and the vanishing rural world; the poacher and the field as the moral centre; the household of women and the war; the airman behind the lines and the occupied country; the county as the world entire.
historical_significance: H. E. Bates is the novelist of the English country and of the airman's war: The Poacher carried the country novel into the 1930s and Fair Stood the Wind for France is the most read novel of the airman behind the lines.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the short-story writer of the strange and the everyday
literary_identity: Short-story writer and poet; the author of Adam and Eve and Pinch Me and The Field of Mustard.
biography: Born Alfred Edgar Coppard at Folkestone on 4 January 1878; he left school at nine and worked as a clerk and a machine salesman until the stories of Adam and Eve and Pinch Me (1921) made him a writer. The Black Dog and Other Stories (1923) and The Field of Mustard (1926) fixed his manner of the strange in the everyday, and his Collected Tales of 1948 made him one of the masters of the English short story; he died at Oxford on 13 January 1957.
literary_profile: A. E. Coppard is among the masters of the English short story between the wars: his tales of the strange in the everyday - the black dog, the field of mustard, the fair and the funeral - carried the wonder-tale into the village and the market, and his verse of the country is the companion to the stories.
stylistic_characteristics: The short story of the single strange turn in the everyday; the village, the fair and the market of the southern counties; the prose of the spoken rhythm and the sudden image; the ballad and the country lyric in verse; the deadpan of the teller who does not explain.
intellectual_concerns: The strange in the everyday; the village and the fair of the southern country; poverty and the clerk's life self-taught; the ballad and the wonder-tale as the form of the modern story; the unexplained as the moral centre.
historical_significance: A. E. Coppard is among the masters of the English short story between the wars: his tales of the strange in the everyday carried the wonder-tale into the village and the market, and his Collected Tales fixed his place in the form.
